sections.h2: What counts as an Ohio land installment contract
sections.html:
In Ohio it is an executory agreement, not fully performed within a year, in which the seller agrees to convey title and the buyer pays the price in installments while the seller holds title as security. Chapter 5313 of the Revised Code covers it, and R.C. 5313.01 sets the terms. The chapter calls the seller the vendor and the buyer the vendee.

Two limits in the definitions matter. The property must be Ohio real property improved by a dwelling, so a bare lot sale falls outside the chapter. And an option contract to buy real property is expressly not a land installment contract.

The seller can be almost anyone: an individual, partnership, corporation, association, trust, or any other group. An investor who sells on contract is covered by the same chapter as a homeowner who sells to a neighbor.

The contract is signed in duplicate, and each side keeps a copy. R.C. 5313.02 then lists sixteen items the document must contain at a minimum. The main ones:

  • Full names and current mailing addresses of all parties, and the date each party signed.
  • A legal description of the property, the contract price, any separate service charges, the down payment, and the resulting principal balance.
  • The amount and due date of each installment, plus the interest rate on the unpaid balance and how it is computed.
  • A statement of encumbrances against the property and of any pending order of a public agency.
  • A promise to deliver a general warranty deed on completion, or another available deed if a general warranty deed is not possible.
  • A provision that the seller supply evidence of title under local custom.
  • A provision that, if the seller defaults on a mortgage, the buyer may pay it and get credit on the contract.
  • A provision that the seller will have the contract recorded, and a term making the buyer responsible for taxes and assessments from the contract date unless the parties agree otherwise.

The seller cannot carry a mortgage larger than the balance due on the contract, unless the mortgage covers additional property and the seller disclosed the amount and release price in writing. A seller also cannot place a larger mortgage without the buyer's consent. If the legal description is by metes and bounds, the county engineer reviews it and marks approval on the contract.

The seller must have a copy recorded under R.C. 5301.25 within twenty days after both parties sign, and must deliver a copy to the county auditor. Recording puts the buyer's interest on the public record at the county recorder, which protects the buyer if the seller later sells or borrows against the same house.

The contract must also follow the formalities Ohio law requires for deeds and mortgages. Each county recorder has its own fee schedule and filing instructions, so call the recorder where the property sits for current requirements.

One duty continues after signing. At least once a year, or on the buyer's demand no more than twice a year, the seller must furnish a statement showing the amount credited to principal and interest and the balance due. A land contract passbook issued by the seller or a financial institution satisfies this. If a seller ignores the chapter, R.C. 5313.04 lets the buyer enforce it in a municipal court, county court or court of common pleas.

The seller starts by waiting out the cure period. Under R.C. 5313.05, forfeiture can be enforced only after thirty days from the date of default, and a buyer who pays everything currently due, with any charges, inside that window avoids forfeiture.

After the thirty days, the seller serves a written notice. Under R.C. 5313.06 it must identify the contract and the property, list the terms not met, and state that the contract stands forfeited unless the buyer performs within ten days of completed service. It must also tell the buyer to leave. Service can be by hand, by leaving it at the usual home or at the property, or by registered or certified mail to the last known address.

The route after that depends on how far the buyer has paid:

  • Under five years in, the seller may sue for forfeiture and restitution of the property under Chapter 1923, and serving the 5313.06 notice satisfies the three-day notice rule in R.C. 1923.04(A).
  • At five years of payments, or twenty percent of the price paid, the seller can recover possession only through foreclosure and a judicial sale under R.C. 2323.07.
  • In that sale the seller takes proceeds up to the unpaid contract balance.

A judgment for the seller cancels the contract as of a date the court sets. The court clerk sends a certified copy to the county recorder, who records it as an instrument of cancellation. Ending the contract this way is the seller's exclusive remedy, with one exception: if the buyer paid less than fair rental value plus damage to the property, the seller may recover the difference.

Key periods in Ohio Revised Code Chapter 5313
StepPeriod
Record the contract and deliver a copy to the auditor (5313.02(C))Within 20 days after both sign
Statement of balance to buyer (5313.03)At least yearly, no more than twice a year on demand
Cure period after a missed payment (5313.05)30 days from default
Forfeiture notice cure window (5313.06(C))10 days from completed service

A seller who wants to end a contract should check each period against the current statute before sending anything.

sections.h2: Disclosures and sale issues on a land contract house
sections.html:
The residential property disclosure form in R.C. 5302.30 applies to transfers of one-to-four unit residential property made by sale, land installment contract, lease with option to purchase, exchange, or a 99-year renewable lease. A seller on contract completes the form and delivers it to the prospective buyer as soon as practicable. Exempt transfers include those by court order, by a fiduciary administering an estate, between spouses or to lineal relatives, and to a buyer who has lived in the property for a year or more, along with a few others.

If the buyer gets the form or an amendment after signing, the buyer has three business days to rescind in writing, and the right ends by the earlier of thirty days after acceptance or closing. A buyer who never receives the form after making an offer may also rescind within that same outer limit.

Owners who want out of a land contract situation have a few starting points. A seller who holds title and wants to sell the house outright will need the recorded contract, the payment history, and the mortgage payoff. A buyer in default who has paid for several years should talk to a lawyer before leaving, since the five-year and twenty-percent rules can change what the seller may do. Both sides can also cancel their interest together by an instrument recorded under R.C. 5301.331, which Chapter 5313 leaves available.

When a seller on contract wants to cash out, the buyer's rights come first. A cash purchaser will want to see the recorded contract, the payment history and proof of where the buyer stands, and will usually need the buyer's signed release before the deal can close. Gather those papers before you call anyone.

faqs.q: How long does an Ohio land contract buyer have to cure a missed payment?
faqs.a: Thirty days from the date of default. Paying all amounts currently due plus any contract fees within that period stops forfeiture, per R.C. 5313.05.

faqs.q: Can an Ohio seller evict a land contract buyer who has paid for years?
faqs.a: Not by forfeiture alone once the buyer has paid for five years or has paid twenty percent of the price. At that point the seller must use foreclosure and judicial sale under R.C. 2323.07.

faqs.q: Does an Ohio land contract have to be recorded?
faqs.a: Yes. The seller must cause a copy to be recorded and delivered to the county auditor within twenty days after both parties sign, under R.C. 5313.02(C).

faqs.q: What notice does an Ohio seller give before forfeiture?
faqs.a: A written notice that names the contract and property, lists the unmet terms, says the contract is forfeited unless the buyer performs within ten days of service, and tells the buyer to leave. R.C. 5313.06 sets those contents.

faqs.q: Can I rent out or sell a house I am buying on land contract in Ohio?
faqs.a: That depends on the contract terms and the seller's recorded title, which Chapter 5313 leaves to the written agreement. Ask a real estate attorney and the county recorder before listing.
